name: Baricitinib

lead: Baricitinib is a once-daily pill approved for severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition causing patchy or total hair loss. Hair communities follow it for its regrowth results, and in June 2022 the FDA approved it as the first systemic treatment for severe alopecia areata in adults.

It blocks JAK1 and JAK2 enzymes, which relay inflammatory cytokine signals, calming the immune attack on follicles so they can resume growth. In the BRAVE-AA1 and BRAVE-AA2 phase 3 trials, more people regrew hair than on placebo at the higher dose. It has not been tested or approved for common male pattern baldness.

paras: It is a prescription pill taken daily under medical supervision, with regular monitoring of blood counts, lipids and liver tests. Regrowth is assessed over months of treatment.

The label carries a boxed warning for serious infections, mortality, cancer, major cardiovascular events and blood clots. It is a prescription medicine, and the trial evidence applies to alopecia areata only.

angle.text: Baricitinib is a prescription JAK inhibitor approved for severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition causing patchy or total hair loss. It calms the immune attack so follicles resume growth and patches fill in. Two phase 3 trials showed regrowth over placebo; it is not approved for ordinary male pattern baldness.

lead: Baricitinib (brand name Olumiant) is an oral Janus kinase (JAK) 1 and 2 inhibitor developed by Incyte and Eli Lilly and approved for rheumatoid arthritis, severe alopecia areata and hospitalised COVID-19.[1][2] For hair, it is relevant to alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition causing patchy or total hair loss that can include eyebrows and eyelashes, rather than to common male pattern baldness.[3][4][5]

Hair loss from alopecia areata can reach the scalp, eyebrows, eyelashes and beard, which is why regrowth on treatment is often described in terms of the whole face and not only the scalp. Baricitinib was the first oral JAK inhibitor approved for the condition, and it was followed by ritlecitinib (June 2023) and deuruxolitinib (July 2024).[6][7][8]

In June 2022 the FDA approved baricitinib as the first systemic treatment for severe alopecia areata in adults, based on the BRAVE-AA1 and BRAVE-AA2 phase 3 trials, in which a substantial share of patients on the higher dose regrew most of their scalp hair by week 36.[1][5]

Alopecia areata can have a large effect on appearance and quality of life, and a European consensus notes that baricitinib and ritlecitinib are the only two EMA-approved medications for it.[3] It is a prescription immunosuppressant and carries a boxed warning for serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events and thrombosis.[1][9]

The wider class of JAK inhibitors, with ruxolitinib reported in 2014 to restore hair in three people with long-standing severe disease, is the background to the drug's use in alopecia areata.[6] Online discussion of baricitinib is mostly found in alopecia areata patient communities and dermatology news rather than in male pattern baldness circles, where the drug is not indicated.

paras: Baricitinib is indicated for moderately to severely active rheumatoid arthritis after inadequate response to TNF antagonists, for severe alopecia areata, and for hospitalised adults with COVID-19 requiring supplemental oxygen or ventilation.[1] It has also been studied in atopic dermatitis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis and vitiligo,[10][11] and JAK inhibitors for rheumatoid arthritis are reviewed.[12] A European guideline on atopic eczema covers its place among systemic therapies.[13]

A European consensus defines a SALT score of 20 or higher as a commonly accepted indication for systemic therapy in alopecia areata, and lists baricitinib for adults among two EMA-approved options, with glucocorticoids, cyclosporine, methotrexate and azathioprine used off-label.[3] The FDA approval in June 2022 applies to adults with at least 50 percent scalp hair loss (SALT 50 or higher) lasting more than six months.[1]

The SALT score measures scalp hair loss from 0 (none) to 100 (complete). Alopecia areata can progress from limited patches to complete scalp (totalis) and body (universalis) hair loss, and children with the condition often experience bullying, according to the European consensus.[3]

Alopecia areata is understood as an autoimmune disease in which immune cells gather around hair follicles in their growing phase. Follicles are normally shielded by a state called immune privilege, and the condition is attributed to a breach of that privilege.[6] Roughly 0.15 percent of people are affected at any one time and about 2 percent at some point in life, with onset usually in childhood.[6]

Patchy cases often regrow on their own within months to a year. Wikipedia reports that among people who lose all body hair, fewer than 10 percent recover without treatment, and that the condition does not shorten life or impair body function but can bring loss of self-image, anxiety and depression.[6] The European expert consensus notes that children and adolescents with the condition often experience bullying.[3]

The variants that matter for appearance include alopecia totalis (all scalp hair), alopecia universalis (all body hair) and ophiasis (a band around the edge of the scalp), as well as eyebrow, eyelash and beard involvement.[6] Hair-restoration options such as transplants have been reported to fall out again when the disease recurs, one reason that immune-directed treatment is of interest.[6]

In practice baricitinib is taken as a once-daily tablet under dermatologist supervision, and the label specifies baseline screening and periodic blood tests.[1] Regrowth is gradual: the pivotal trials measured the primary outcome at 36 weeks, and the National Alopecia Areata Foundation (NAAF) says some people respond later than others.[5][14] NAAF reports that about 32 to 35 percent of people with extensive disease on the higher dose reached 80 percent or more scalp coverage at 36 weeks, and that around 90 percent of those continuing for two years reached that level in trials.[14]

The approval covers adults with severe disease (at least 50 percent scalp hair loss, lasting more than six months).[1] Because the trials measured scalp coverage, much of the data concerns the scalp, while patients and clinicians also track eyebrows and eyelashes, which matter for facial appearance.[3][5] The drug is not indicated for male or female pattern hair loss, and the research on baricitinib is confined to immune-mediated conditions.[1]

Other systemic treatments used off-label for alopecia areata in Europe include glucocorticoids, cyclosporine, methotrexate and azathioprine, and the European consensus describes oral minoxidil as an adjuvant with limited supporting data.[3] Generic tofacitinib, a related JAK inhibitor approved for rheumatoid arthritis, is described by NAAF as being prescribed off-label by some dermatologists.[15]

JAK inhibitors block Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2), which relay signals from more than fifty cytokines inside immune cells.[7] Ruxolitinib was approved in 2011 for myelofibrosis, tofacitinib in 2012, and baricitinib in the EU in February 2017.[7] After the 2014 report of hair regrowth in three people on ruxolitinib, the class was developed for alopecia areata.[6]

Ritlecitinib, which inhibits JAK3 and TEC-family kinases, was approved in the US in June 2023, the EU in September 2023 and Canada in November 2023 for people aged 12 and older with severe alopecia areata; its ALLEGRO-2b/3 trial randomised 718 participants.[3][8] Deuruxolitinib (a JAK1/2 inhibitor) followed in the US in July 2024.[6][14] No head-to-head trial of baricitinib against ritlecitinib has been reported in published summaries of ritlecitinib.[8]

The BRAVE-AA1 and BRAVE-AA2 phase 3 randomised trials, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2022, compared baricitinib 2 mg and 4 mg with placebo in adults with severe alopecia areata. In BRAVE-AA1 (654 patients), 38.8 percent on 4 mg, 22.8 percent on 2 mg and 6.2 percent on placebo reached a SALT score of 20 or lower at week 36; in BRAVE-AA2 (546 patients) the figures were 35.9, 19.4 and 3.3 percent.[5] A later analysis from BRAVE-AA1 examined withdrawal and retreatment in patients with severe disease.[16] A short commentary on baricitinib for alopecia areata was also published.

The boxed warning covers serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events and thrombosis, with screening for tuberculosis and monitoring of blood counts, lipids and liver enzymes.[1] Common effects include upper respiratory infections, headache, nausea and raised cholesterol, and live vaccines are contraindicated.[1] In studies upper respiratory infections and high cholesterol occurred in more than 10 percent of participants, with herpes zoster, herpes simplex, urinary tract infections and gastroenteritis less common; use in pregnancy is contraindicated.[2]

In September 2021 the FDA issued a Drug Safety Communication requiring boxed warnings for tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib on serious heart-related events, cancer, blood clots and death. The warning followed a required safety trial of tofacitinib in rheumatoid arthritis patients aged 50 or older with a cardiovascular risk factor, which found higher rates than with TNF blockers; the FDA said baricitinib was not studied in a similar trial but may carry similar risks because the mechanism is shared.[17]

The FDA listed people at higher risk as current or past smokers and those with prior heart attack, stroke, blood clots or other cardiovascular risk factors.[17] The European Medicines Agency's safety committee recommended that these medicines be used only when no suitable alternative exists in people aged 65 or older, those at higher cardiovascular or cancer risk, and current or long-term former smokers.[7] JAK-inhibitor labelling also notes a raised risk of varicella-zoster infection, so vaccination status is typically checked beforehand.[7]

Baricitinib competitively inhibits JAK1 and JAK2 enzymes, disrupting JAK-STAT signalling by which several inflammatory cytokines act, including in joints, skin and hair follicles.[1] Alopecia areata is understood as an immune attack on hair follicles, which is the rationale for JAK inhibition.[3] Reported IC50 values are about 5.9 nM for JAK1 and 5.7 nM for JAK2, with weaker activity on TYK2 and JAK3.[2]

Oral bioavailability is about 79 percent, peak plasma levels occur around one hour after a dose, food has no relevant effect, and less than 10 percent is metabolised by CYP3A4; the half-life is about 12.5 hours, with about 75 percent excreted in urine.[2]

Incyte discovered baricitinib and licensed it to Eli Lilly.[2] The European Commission approved it for rheumatoid arthritis in February 2017; Lilly filed a US application in January 2016, received a rejection in April 2017 citing dosing and safety, and the FDA approved it on 31 May 2018.[1][2] The FDA granted breakthrough therapy designation for alopecia areata in March 2020.[2]

Emergency use for COVID-19 followed on 19 November 2020, with full approval on 11 May 2022 as the first immunomodulatory COVID-19 treatment, and the alopecia areata approval came in June 2022.[1][2] Its COVID-19 benefit was evaluated in the ACTT-2, COV-BARRIER and RECOVERY trials and in animal models.[18][19][20]

Phase 3 evidence for alopecia areata comes from BRAVE-AA1 and BRAVE-AA2,[5] with a withdrawal and retreatment analysis.[16] A registered phase 2 study examined central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia in adults of African descent.[21] Studies in other conditions include rheumatoid arthritis (a 52-week trial of 1,307 patients compared it with placebo and adalimumab),[22][22] juvenile idiopathic arthritis, atopic dermatitis (including extended treatment in children) and vitiligo,[10][11][23] type 1 diabetes,[24] and autoinflammatory interferonopathies.[25] No trials of baricitinib in common male or female pattern hair loss were identified.

Baricitinib is a prescription drug; people with alopecia areata can access it through dermatologists. It sits alongside ritlecitinib as one of the two EMA-approved systemic options for the condition.[3] Because it suppresses immune signalling, its use involves ongoing safety monitoring and a discussion of risks and benefits with a clinician.

NAAF notes that FDA approval does not guarantee insurance coverage: plans may require prior authorisation documenting severity (SALT score), duration and prior treatments, with reviews taking weeks, and common denial reasons include classifying the treatment as cosmetic or step-therapy rules.[15] It reports that Lilly and Pfizer offer bridge programmes during appeals and that insurers sometimes require non-medical switches between JAK inhibitors, a practice NAAF opposes.[15]

Health Canada availability for alopecia areata is described on Wikipedia as through a Lilly patient support programme as of February 2025.[2] Public coverage of the approval has framed alopecia areata as a medical condition with psychosocial burden, and the notable people reported to have the condition include actors, athletes and politicians.[6]

lore.intro: Discussion of baricitinib for hair takes place mainly in alopecia areata patient organisations and dermatology literature; the claims below are those that circulate among patients and advocates, stated with attribution.[14][15]

claims.claim: Baricitinib can regrow scalp, eyebrow and eyelash hair in severe alopecia areata.
It is also a treatment for ordinary male or female pattern baldness.
Results continue to improve with longer treatment.
The medicine is a lifelong commitment because hair may fall out again.
JAK inhibitors carry serious risks that outweigh cosmetic benefit.
Insurance treats alopecia areata drugs as cosmetic, blocking access.
Cheaper generic tofacitinib is a workable alternative.

timeline.event: Ruxolitinib becomes the first JAK inhibitor approved in the US (myelofibrosis).[7]
Preliminary reports show oral ruxolitinib restoring hair in three people with severe alopecia areata.[6]
EU approves baricitinib for rheumatoid arthritis (February); the US application is rejected in April.[2]
FDA approves baricitinib for rheumatoid arthritis on 31 May.[1][2]
Breakthrough designation for alopecia areata (March); COVID-19 emergency use authorisation (November).[2]
FDA Drug Safety Communication (1 September) adds boxed warnings for JAK inhibitors including baricitinib.[17]
BRAVE-AA1 and BRAVE-AA2 published; FDA approves baricitinib for COVID-19 (May) and severe alopecia areata (June).[1][5]
FDA approves ritlecitinib for alopecia areata in June, EU in September.[8]
European consensus names baricitinib and ritlecitinib as the two EMA-approved systemic options; FDA approves deuruxolitinib in July.[3][6]
